respondent: Director, Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs, United States Department of Labor; Karen Vena Mullins, on behalf of the Estate of Roger L. Mullins
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
facts: Roger Mullins filed a claim for Black Lung benefits in 2012, alleging total disability due to pulmonary disease caused by coal dust. After initial denial, Mullins filed a request for modification in 2019, claiming a mistake of fact and changed conditions. The ALJ granted the modification, finding Mullins totally disabled due to legal pneumoconiosis and awarding benefits. Cedar Coal Company, Mullins' last coal mine employer, appealed to the Benefits Review Board (BRB), which affirmed the award.
conclusion: The court disagreed with Cedar Coal Company's contentions that Mullins presented excessive affirmative evidence and that the ALJ's finding of legal pneumoconiosis lacked substantial evidence. The court found that the ALJ's decision was supported by substantial evidence, including medical reports and treatment records. The court emphasized the distinction between clinical and legal pneumoconiosis, and the regulations governing evidence submission in black lung benefit claims.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
facts: John McLaurin pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute cocaine and was sentenced to 120 months imprisonment and five years of supervised release. At the sentencing hearing, the district court orally recited four special conditions of release but did not mention any standard conditions. The written judgment contained both the special conditions and fourteen standard conditions. McLaurin's supervised release was later revoked based on violations of standard conditions that were in the written judgment but not pronounced orally at sentencing.
conclusion: The Fourth Circuit held that under United States v. Rogers, a district court must orally pronounce all non-mandatory conditions of supervised release at the sentencing hearing, and any discretionary conditions appearing only in the written judgment are nullities. The court found that McLaurin's appellate waiver did not bar the Rogers challenge and that the appeal was timely and procedurally proper. The court concluded that the district court erred in revoking supervised release based on conditions that were never properly imposed.

case_name: Fritz Emmanuel Lesly Miot v. Donald Trump
petitioner: Donald J. Trump, President of the United States of America, et al.
respondent: Fritz Emmanuel Lesly Miot, et al.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit
facts: Haitian nationals holding Temporary Protected Status (TPS) sued after the Department of Homeland Security terminated Haiti's TPS designation. The district court postponed the termination, finding it arbitrary and capricious, contrary to the TPS statute, and in violation of the Fifth Amendment's equal protection guarantee. The government sought a stay pending appeal, arguing that the district court's order was an improper intrusion into the workings of the executive branch. The government relied on Supreme Court stay orders in a similar TPS case, National TPS Alliance v. Noem.
conclusion: The court denied the motion for a stay pending appeal. The court found that the government failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, as it did not name a single concrete harm from maintaining the status quo. The court distinguished the case from National TPS Alliance v. Noem, where the government asserted a concrete and imminent harm related to ongoing negotiations with Venezuela, which was absent in this case. The court found the government's generalized assertions of injury insufficient to support a stay.

respondent: Grieg Star AS; Grieg Maritime Group AS; Grieg Foundation
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
facts: Balvina Renteria, a longshore worker, was injured when she fell through plastic sheeting covering a gap between cargo rolls on the M/V Star Juventas. Grieg Star AS was the vessel's technical manager. Renteria was employed by Cooper/Ports America and was assigned to roll up the plastic sheeting when the accident occurred. She received instructions from the stevedore and had no communication with the vessel's crew. Renteria sued Grieg Star for vessel negligence under the LHWCA.
conclusion: The court reviewed the district court's grant of summary judgment de novo, applying the same standard as the district court. The court considered the turnover duty, which requires the vessel owner to exercise ordinary care to turn over the ship in a safe condition and to warn of latent dangers. The court found that the condition was open and obvious, and the stevedore was in the best position to discover and avoid the hazard.

petitioner: Brown-Forman Corporation, dba Woodford Reserve Distillery
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
facts: Employees at Brown-Forman's Woodford Reserve facility sought unionization due to dissatisfaction with wages. In response to the organizing campaign, Brown-Forman announced increased employee compensation. The union failed to secure a majority vote in the election. An Administrative Law Judge determined that Brown-Forman committed unfair labor practices and interfered with unionization efforts, recommending a bargaining order based on Cemex and Gissel standards. The Board adopted the ALJ's findings but relied solely on the Cemex standard.
conclusion: The court held that the Cemex standard was created through an improper exercise of the Board's adjudicatory authority and cannot serve as the basis for a bargaining order. The court reasoned that the Board's reliance solely on the Cemex standard was improper. Therefore, the court granted Brown-Forman's petition for review, denied the Board's cross-petition for enforcement, and remanded for proceedings consistent with the opinion.

case_name: HPIL Holding, Inc. v. Harry Zhang
respondent: Harry Zhang aka Haining Zhang; Stephen Brown; Angela Collette; David Postula; Brown Family Investments, Ltd.; Crank Media, Inc.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
facts: HPIL Holding sued minority shareholders and others, alleging they looted the corporation during a state-court receivership proceeding. The district court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1257(a), citing the Rooker-Feldman doctrine. The suit stemmed from a state court's appointment of a receiver for HPIL after a complaint by Zhang, a minority shareholder, alleging mismanagement. HPIL claimed Zhang and Collette diluted the corporation's stock and entered an agreement to sell a large portion of it to Brown.
conclusion: The court held that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine did not apply because HPIL did not seek to appeal the state-court appointment of a receiver. The jurisdictional bar under § 1257(a) is narrow and does not displace customary preclusion principles. The court reasoned that the district court erred in dismissing the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, as the lawsuit did not constitute a direct appeal of a state court decision.

case_name: Marquetta Williams v. City of Canton, Ohio
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
facts: On New Year's Day in Canton, Ohio, James Williams fired a rifle into the air from his enclosed patio. Officer Robert Huber arrived to investigate and, without warning, fatally shot Williams through the fence. Williams's wife sued, and Huber asserted a qualified-immunity defense. The district court denied summary judgment to Huber, finding a factual dispute for a jury to decide.
conclusion: The court held that a jury must decide the key factual dispute: whether Huber saw Williams turning the rifle toward him or firing into the air. If Williams was turning the rifle toward Huber, the shooting would be justified. However, if Williams was firing into the air, Huber would have violated the Fourth Amendment because he lacked probable cause to believe that Williams posed a threat. The court reasoned that a reasonable officer would recognize that shooting a man without warning for discharging a gun into the air, a misdemeanor in Canton, violates the Fourth Amendment.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
facts: Jerome Brown was indicted for drug trafficking and illegally possessing a firearm after a law enforcement raid. He entered plea negotiations with the Government, and the parties presented two different stipulated plea agreements to the District Court. The District Court rejected both pleas, and proposed its own sentence. Brown ultimately entered an open guilty plea and received a sentence of 235 months' imprisonment.
conclusion: The District Court violated Rule 11(c)(1) by engaging in plea negotiations and inducing Brown to accept a plea of not less than 235 months. However, Brown failed to demonstrate that the error affected his substantial rights, as he consistently intended to plead guilty. Therefore, the court affirmed the lower court's decision.

case_name: Christopher Massey v. Borough of Bergenfield
respondent: Borough of Bergenfield, Arvin Amatorio, Hernandez Rivera, Ora Kornbluth, Rafael Marte, Buddy Deauna
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
facts: Christopher Massey, a white male, was denied a promotion to Chief of Police in the Borough of Bergenfield in favor of Mustafa Rabboh, an Arab-Muslim male. Massey brought discrimination claims under state and federal law. The District Court granted summary judgment for the defendants. The central issue involves New Jersey's "Background Circumstances Rule," which places a heightened burden on plaintiffs who are not in the "minority."
conclusion: The court predicted that the Supreme Court of New Jersey would rely on Ames v. Ohio Dep't of Youth Servs. to conclude that the State’s Background Circumstances Rule no longer has a permissible role to play in litigation under New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD). The Rule is incompatible with the operative text of the NJLAD, which is identical to the pertinent language from Title VII. After removing the Background Circumstances Rule, there are genuine disputes concerning material facts that arise from Plaintiff’s direct and circumstantial evidence of discrimination.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
facts: Kyle Aguilar was convicted of two counts of Abusive Sexual Contact in Indian Country involving his niece, P.C. The charges stemmed from an incident where Aguilar allegedly touched P.C.'s genitalia and breasts. Aguilar appealed, arguing that the two convictions for the same incident violated the Double Jeopardy Clause and that there was insufficient evidence to support the convictions. P.C. testified to the incidents, describing the touching and her reactions.
conclusion: The court concluded that the convictions were not multiplicitous and did not violate the Double Jeopardy Clause. It also found that there was sufficient evidence to support Aguilar's convictions, based on P.C.'s testimony and other evidence presented at trial. The court reasoned that the touching of different body parts constituted separate offenses under the relevant statutes.

case_name: Jones v. City of North Las Vegas
respondent: City of North Las Vegas; Scott Salkoff; Michael Rose
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
facts: Police officers responded to a domestic battery call and one officer saw a suspect flee into a neighboring backyard. The officer lost sight of the suspect for at least eighteen minutes before a K-9 unit alerted in the direction of the plaintiffs' backyard. An officer searched the yard, and two of the plaintiffs' dogs attacked the police K-9 and were shot and killed. The plaintiffs sued, claiming the officers and the City of North Las Vegas violated their Fourth Amendment rights.
conclusion: The court held that there was no hot pursuit because officers lost track of the suspect for at least eighteen minutes, thus the officers were not entitled to qualified immunity. The court found that the officer's use of force was reasonable under the circumstances. The court also found no support for the plaintiffs' failure-to-train theory against the city.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
facts: Andrew Butler pled guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm. Police responded to a 911 call from Jasmine Spates, who reported that Butler broke into her apartment with a gun. Officers knew Butler was a convicted felon with outstanding misdemeanor arrest warrants and was on probation with a warrantless search waiver. Officers found Butler at his workplace, Altium Packaging. After Butler ran and refused to drop a gun, officers apprehended him and charged him with firearm offenses.
conclusion: The court held that even assuming Butler had a reasonable expectation of privacy at his workplace, he could not challenge the officers' entry because the Steagald case only addressed the rights of a third party not named in the arrest warrant to the privacy of their home. The court also found that the district court did not abuse its discretion in sentencing Butler, as it considered relevant factors and did not give significant weight to improper factors. The court reasoned that the district court's consideration of the seriousness of the offense, the need for deterrence, and Butler's history were appropriate.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
facts: James Beeler pled guilty to possession of child pornography. The district court determined Beeler was subject to a 10-year mandatory minimum sentence due to his prior Missouri conviction for abuse of a child. Beeler was sentenced to 120 months’ imprisonment followed by a lifetime of supervised release. Beeler appealed his sentence, claiming the district court improperly applied the sentencing enhancement and violated due process.
conclusion: The Eighth Circuit held that Beeler's prior conviction under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 568.060.1(2) "relates to" child pornography as defined under federal law, triggering the mandatory minimum sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 2252A(b)(2). The court reasoned that even if state and federal law do not prohibit exactly the same conduct, the state conviction broadly pertains to, is connected with, or stands in some relation to the federal offense. The court also rejected Beeler's argument that § 2252A(b)(2) is unconstitutionally vague.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
facts: Julian Sandoval-Flores pleaded guilty to attempted murder and violating 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) after shooting at law enforcement officers. He later sought relief under 28 U.S.C. § 2255, arguing that his § 924(c) conviction was based on the unconstitutional residual clause. The district court denied his motion, finding that his collateral-attack waiver barred relief and that he failed to show the sentencing court relied on the residual clause. Sandoval-Flores appealed the denial of his § 2255 motion.
conclusion: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Sandoval-Flores's § 2255 motion, exercising jurisdiction under § 2255(d). The court agreed with the lower court that Sandoval-Flores failed to establish by a preponderance of the evidence that the trial court relied on the unconstitutional residual clause in convicting him under § 924(c).

case_name: Fredis Ortez Reyes v. United States Citizenship and Immigration Services
respondent: United States Citizenship and Immigration Services; Ur M. Jaddou; Ted H. Kim; Kimberly Zanotti
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
facts: Fredis Ortez Reyes, a Honduran native and asylee, filed a Form I-730 petition for his wife, Gloria Magaly Estrada Moreno, to receive derivative asylee status. USCIS denied the petition based on Section 1231(a)(5) of the INA, which bars relief for noncitizens with prior removal orders, as Ms. Estrada had been previously removed. Reyes challenged this decision in district court, arguing that Section 1231(a)(5) should not apply to I-730 petitions governed by 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3)(A). The district court dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction, finding the USCIS decision was a discretionary act not subject to judicial review.
conclusion: The court held that Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) does not preclude judicial review of a decision to deny discretionary relief when the decision was based solely on the USCIS's interpretation of the INA. Pure decisions of law fall outside the scope of the jurisdiction-stripping statute. The USCIS's decision was based on statutory interpretation, not an exercise of discretion considering the specific circumstances of the petitioner. Therefore, the court has jurisdiction to review the USCIS's decision.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
facts: Sergio Carrillo Murillo, a lawful permanent resident, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute cocaine, an aggravated felony that made him subject to mandatory deportation. He filed a § 2255 motion, claiming ineffective assistance of counsel because his lawyer allegedly failed to advise him about the deportation consequences. The district court initially denied the motion, but the Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded. On remand, the district court again rejected Carrillo's claim, finding he failed to establish deficient performance by his counsel.
conclusion: The court held that Carrillo failed to demonstrate that his counsel's performance was deficient under the Strickland standard. The court considered the plea agreement's provision acknowledging potential immigration consequences and the statements made during the plea hearing. Based on these factors, the court concluded that Carrillo did not establish that his counsel's performance fell below an objective standard of reasonableness.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
facts: Lester Landrum was convicted for possession of a firearm after a felony conviction in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). He was indicted for possessing the weapon on November 12, 2023. Landrum's prior felonies include convictions for drug trafficking and a DUI offense. He challenged his conviction, arguing that § 922(g)(1) is unconstitutionally vague.
conclusion: The court held that Landrum's vagueness argument failed because the statute itself, § 922(g)(1), clearly defines the prohibited conduct as possessing a firearm as a felon. The court also noted that Landrum's other arguments were foreclosed by precedent. The court found that Kimble and Giglio meant he could be constitutionally disarmed pursuant to the Second Amendment. Therefore, the court affirmed the conviction.

case_name: United States v. Michael Shane Ragland
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
facts: Michael Ragland was convicted of multiple federal crimes related to armed robberies and sentenced to 196 years. He successfully moved to vacate one count, leading to a resentencing of 173 years. Ragland appealed, arguing for resentencing under the First Step Act (FSA), but the District Court denied this. Following a Supreme Court decision in Hewitt v. United States, Ragland petitioned for rehearing, arguing that he should be resentenced under the FSA.
conclusion: The court granted Ragland's petition for rehearing in part, specifically vacating and replacing Part II.B of its prior opinion regarding the retroactivity of the FSA. It also affirmed and clarified Part III of that opinion to highlight a potential circuit split. The court reasoned that the Supreme Court's decision in Hewitt was binding and required reconsideration of the FSA's applicability to Ragland's case.

respondent: Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, Secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security; Ur M. Jaddou, Director of U.S. Citizenship & Immigration Services (USCIS); United States Citizenship and Immigration Services; Laura Zuchowski, Director of the Vermont Service Center of USCIS
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
facts: Sosimo Vera Chairez, a citizen of Mexico, applied for a U visa, which is available to victims of certain crimes who have suffered abuse and are helpful to law enforcement. Chairez was inadmissible to the United States but sought a waiver of inadmissibility from USCIS, which was denied. He then sued in district court under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging that the denial of the waiver was unlawful. The district court dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
conclusion: The court held that the agency's denial of a waiver of inadmissibility under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(d)(14) falls within 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii), which precludes judicial review of agency action when the authority is specified to be in the discretion of the Secretary. The court found that the statute uses permissive language and that the Secretary's consideration of the national or public interest reinforces its discretionary nature. The court also rejected the argument that 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D) provides jurisdiction, as it only preserves review in petitions for review from a final order of removal. Finally, the court found that the plaintiff's constitutional claim was speculative and not colorable.

petitioner: Donald J. Trump, in his official capacity as President of the United States; Marco Rubio, in his official capacity as Secretary of State; Kristi Noem, in her official capacity as Secretary of Homeland Security; Robert F. Kennedy Jr., in his official capacity as Secretary of Health and Human Services
respondent: Pacito; Esther; Josephine; Sara; Alyas; Marcos; Ahmed; Rachel; Ali; HIAS, INC.; CHURCH WORLD SERVICE, INC.; LUTHERAN COMMUNITY SERVICES NORTHWEST
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
facts: This case concerns Executive Order No. 14163, which suspended the United States Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) and related funding. The plaintiffs challenged the executive order, arguing it exceeded the President's statutory authority and violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The district court granted preliminary injunctions prohibiting enforcement of the executive order. The government appealed, arguing that the claims were unreviewable and that the executive order was within the President's authority.
conclusion: The panel affirmed in part and reversed in part the district court's preliminary injunctions. The panel concluded that the plaintiffs failed to show a likelihood of success on the merits of their challenges to the executive order as beyond the President's statutory authority. However, the panel agreed with the district court that the government likely acted contrary to law by failing to provide statutorily mandated services to refugees already admitted to the United States and that the termination of cooperative agreements with resettlement support centers was likely arbitrary and capricious.

case_name: Monica Perkins v. City of Des Moines
respondent: City of Des Moines; Dana Wingert; Rodell Nydam; Scott Newman; Jason Tart
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
facts: Monica Perkins sued the City of Des Moines and several police officials, including Deputy Jason Tart, after she was struck in the hand by a less-lethal impact round fired by Deputy Tart during a protest-turned-riot in May 2020. Perkins alleged excessive force, substantive due process violations, and failure to intervene. The district court granted summary judgment in favor of the defendants. Perkins appealed the district court's decision.
conclusion: The Eighth Circuit reviewed the district court's grant of summary judgment de novo. The court determined that the district court did not err in granting summary judgment on the excessive force claim, the substantive due process claim, and the failure-to-intervene claim. The court reasoned that Perkins was not seized for Fourth Amendment purposes, Deputy Tart's conduct did not shock the conscience, and there was no underlying constitutional violation to support the failure-to-intervene claim.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
facts: Stephen Allen's son died after being pulled into a culvert beneath a bridge on land owned by The Nature Conservancy. Allen sued The Nature Conservancy and its insurers, alleging negligence and malicious failure to warn of an ultra-hazardous condition. The district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The Lydalisk Bridge, where the incident occurred, had underwater currents that accelerated near the culverts' narrow entrances. Allen argued that The Nature Conservancy failed to warn of the danger despite having prior knowledge of similar risks at another bridge.
conclusion: The court determined that the Arkansas Recreational Use Statute (ARUS) limited The Nature Conservancy's duty of care and that Allen had not alleged facts sufficient to prove malicious failure to warn of an ultra-hazardous condition. The court also determined that Arkansas's Direct-Action Statute (DAS) did not authorize Allen to sue the insurers directly because The Nature Conservancy was still subject to suit. Therefore, the court concluded that the district court did not err in dismissing Allen's claims.

court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
facts: Jeremy Kellogg and Jonathan Harmon, New York residents, applied for concealed carry licenses, which were denied by Judge Jonathan D. Nichols, acting as a statutory licensing officer. They sued Judge Nichols under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging that New York's firearms licensing laws violated their Second and Fourteenth Amendment rights. The District Court dismissed the claims, citing absolute immunity for the individual-capacity claims and lack of a case or controversy for the official-capacity claims. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal.
conclusion: The Second Circuit held that judicial officers act in a judicial capacity when deciding firearms license applications and thus enjoy absolute immunity from suit in their individual capacities. The court further held that the plaintiffs' claims for injunctive and declaratory relief against Judge Nichols in his official capacity are barred by Article III's case-or-controversy requirement. The court reasoned that these claims seek review of a state court judge's decision, which is not permissible under Article III.

case_name: Peña Garcia v. Department of Labor
respondent: Director, Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs, United States Department of Labor, IMS Insurance Company of Puerto Rico, Calzadilla Construction Corporation
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
facts: Luis Peña Garcia, a resident of Puerto Rico, sustained work-related injuries in 1994, rendering him permanently disabled. He sought reimbursement for medical cannabis-infused edibles, recommended by his doctor in accordance with Puerto Rico law, to treat his chronic pain. The Department of Labor denied his request, citing marijuana's Schedule I classification under the Controlled Substances Act. The Benefits Review Board affirmed this decision, leading Peña to petition for review.
conclusion: The court held that because marijuana is classified as a Schedule I substance under the Controlled Substances Act, it cannot have any accepted medical use under federal law. Therefore, it cannot be considered a "reasonable and necessary medical treatment" under the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act. The court agreed with the Benefits Review Board's determination that Peña's employer and insurance carrier were not obligated to reimburse him for his cannabis-infused edibles.

case_name: City of Wausau v. Illinois Union Insurance Comapy
respondent: Donald Bouvet; Dorothy Bowman; Doris Box; Georgia Brown; Walter Brown; Scott Champeau; Carol Spiker; Robert Dersham; Catherine Drye; Earl Klinker; Deborah Kostek; Timthoy Leonard; Cathy Loucks; Phillip Marotte; David Martin; Ryan Matthews; Karen McKinney; Ernest Moorer; Megan O'Brien; Zohe Quintero; Cleveland Ross; Darrell Stewart; Krestice Stewart; Lindsay Urena-Tio; William Vonzehle; Pauline Wikkernick; Sy Yost; Mark Zaza; City of Wausau

The plaintiffs, including Donald Bouvet, Dorothy Bowman, and the City of Wausau, brought suit against numerous defendants, including Illinois Union Insurance Company. respondent: Donald Bouvet; Dorothy Bowman; Doris Box; Georgia Brown; Walter Brown; Scott Champeau; Carol Spiker; Robert Dersham; Catherine Drye; Earl Klinker; Deborah Kostek; Timthoy Leonard; Cathy Loucks; Phillip Marotte; David Martin; Ryan Matthews; Karen McKinney; Ernest Moorer; Megan O'Brien; Zohe Quintero; Cleveland Ross; Darrell Stewart; Krestice Stewart; Lindsay Urena-Tio; William Vonzehle; Pauline Wikkernick; Sy Yost; Mark Zaza; City of Wausau
